title: 2.9.7 Compiling C to Assembly, and Compiling and Linking Assembly and C Code

questions.q: Which gcc command-line option tells gcc to compile a C file into an assembly text file (.s)?
questions.explain: -S compiles to assembly, so gcc -m32 -S simpleops.c creates simpleops.s. -c produces a .o object file, -o names the output file, and -m32 selects IA32.

questions.q: What does the -m32 option do in gcc -m32 -S simpleops.c?
choices: Limits the output file to 32 lines
Tells gcc to generate IA32 (32-bit) assembly
Tells gcc to produce a .o object file
questions.explain: -m32 tells gcc to generate IA32 (32-bit x86) code instead of the default.

questions.q: What is the name of the file created by running: gcc -m32 -S simpleops.c
questions.explain: -S writes the compiler's assembly translation to a .s file with the same base name: simpleops.s.

questions.q: The .s file produced by gcc -S is a text file that can be viewed and edited in any text editor.
questions.explain: Assembly (.s) files are plain text. You can open them in an editor such as vim or print them with cat.

questions.q: What does gcc -m32 -c simpleops.s produce?
choices: A relocatable object binary file, simpleops.o
questions.explain: -c assembles the code into binary machine code form: a relocatable object file (.o). It does not link, so it does not produce an executable.

questions.q: In gcc -m32 -o simpleops simpleops.o, what is the role of -o simpleops?
choices: It names the output executable file simpleops
It tells gcc to optimize simpleops.o
It tells gcc to output only assembly
It tells gcc to read simpleops as an object file
questions.explain: -o specifies the name of the output file. Here it is the linked 32-bit executable, simpleops.

questions.q: To link a 32-bit object file into an executable with gcc -m32 -o simpleops simpleops.o, what must be installed on the system?
choices: The 32-bit version of the system libraries
Nothing beyond gcc; 32-bit linking never needs anything extra
questions.explain: Linking a 32-bit executable requires the 32-bit versions of the system libraries.

questions.q: Which command shows the machine code and assembly code mappings in the object file simpleops.o?
questions.explain: objdump -d disassembles a binary file and shows the machine code next to the corresponding assembly instructions.

questions.q: A single gcc command that builds an executable can include both .o files and .c files, which are compiled and linked together.
questions.explain: For example, gcc -m32 -o myprog myfunc.o main.c compiles main.c and links it with myfunc.o into one executable.

questions.q: Only gcc can compile C code to assembly, and only for the IA32 architecture.
questions.explain: Any C compiler can do this, and most compilers can generate several different assembly languages. gcc and IA32 are just the example used here.

questions.q: In simpleops.c (x = 1; x = x + 2; x = x - 14; y = x*100; x = x + y * 6;), what is the final value of y?
In simpleops.c (x = 1; x = x + 2; x = x - 14; y = x*100; x = x + y * 6;), what is the final value of x?

In simpleops.s, what value is stored at -8(%ebp) right after these three instructions run?
  movl $1, -8(%ebp)
  addl $2, -8(%ebp)
  subl $14, -8(%ebp)
questions.explain: The value is set to 1, increased by 2 to 3, then decreased by 14 to -11. This matches x = 1; x = x + 2; x = x - 14.

questions.q: In the generated simpleops.s, where is the local variable x stored?
questions.explain: movl $1, -8(%ebp) implements x = 1, so x is stored at -8(%ebp). y is stored at -4(%ebp), as shown by movl %eax, -4(%ebp) for y = x*100.

questions.q: In simpleops.s, which instruction does the multiplication for y = x*100?
questions.explain: First movl -8(%ebp), %eax loads x into %eax. Then imull $100, %eax, %eax stores x*100 in %eax, and movl %eax, -4(%ebp) saves the result in y.

questions.q:
What does this sequence from simpleops.s compute?
  movl -4(%ebp), %edx
  movl %edx, %eax
  addl %eax, %eax
  addl %edx, %eax
  addl %eax, %eax
  addl %eax, -8(%ebp)
choices: It computes y*100 a second time and stores it in y
It computes x*6 and stores the result in y
It computes y*6 with copies and additions instead of a multiply, then adds the result to x
questions.explain: y goes into %edx and %eax. Then %eax = 2y, then 2y + y = 3y, then 3y + 3y = 6y. Finally 6y is added to x at -8(%ebp), which implements x = x + y * 6.

questions.q: In simpleops.s, after movl -4(%ebp), %edx; movl %edx, %eax; addl %eax, %eax; addl %edx, %eax run, %eax holds y multiplied by what number?
questions.explain: %eax starts as y. addl %eax, %eax makes it 2y, and addl %edx, %eax (with %edx = y) makes it 3y.

questions.q: In simpleops.s, which C statement does movl $0, %eax (just before leave and ret) implement?
questions.explain: In IA32 the function's return value is stored in %eax before returning, so movl $0, %eax sets main's return value to 0.

questions.category: Writing assembly functions and linking with C
questions.q: In an IA32 assembly function such as myfunc, which register should hold the return value before the function returns?
questions.explain: The template says the return value should be stored in %eax before returning.

questions.category: Writing assembly functions and linking with C
questions.q: Which instructions make up the function preamble (stack setup) in the IA32 myfunc template?
questions.explain: The first three instructions (pushl %ebp, movl %esp, %ebp, subl $16, %esp) set up the stack. leave and ret are the return code.

questions.category: Writing assembly functions and linking with C
questions.q: In the IA32 function template, which instructions are the function's return code?
questions.explain: The template ends with leave and ret, which form the function's return code.

questions.category: Writing assembly functions and linking with C
questions.q: In the template for myfunc.s, what does the .text directive at the top indicate?
choices: The file is a plain C source file
The file must be opened in a text editor
questions.explain: As the template's comment says, .text marks that the file contains instruction code.

questions.category: Writing assembly functions and linking with C
questions.q: main.c calls myfunc, which is implemented in assembly in myfunc.s. What must main.c contain to call it?
choices: A copy of myfunc's assembly instructions
The function prototype int myfunc(int param);
Nothing; C code cannot call functions written in assembly
questions.explain: The C program only needs the function prototype. The assembly function is compiled separately and linked in.

questions.category: Writing assembly functions and linking with C
questions.q: Which sequence of commands builds the executable myprog from myfunc.s and main.c?
choices: gcc -m32 -c myfunc.s, then gcc -m32 -o myprog myfunc.o main.c
gcc -m32 -S myfunc.s, then gcc -m32 -o myprog myfunc.s main.o
gcc -m32 -o myfunc.o myfunc.s, then gcc -m32 -c myprog main.c
gcc -m32 -S main.c, then gcc -m32 -c myprog main.s myfunc.s
questions.explain: First, -c turns myfunc.s into the object file myfunc.o. Then gcc compiles main.c and links it with myfunc.o into the executable named by -o myprog.

questions.category: Writing assembly functions and linking with C
questions.q: Every IA32 function uses exactly the same preamble code, no matter how many parameters or local variables it has.
questions.explain: Functions with more parameters or that need more stack space for local variables may have slightly different preamble code.

questions.q: Like C, assembly code is portable: the same assembly code can be compiled and run on many different hardware architectures.
questions.explain: Assembly is very low level and specific to one hardware architecture. C is high level and can be compiled and run on many systems.

questions.q: Which are reasons a programmer might write assembly code by hand?
choices: To write code sequences that are crucial to performance
To access low-level parts of the architecture, such as specific registers
To make the code portable across many hardware architectures
Because compilers cannot translate C into machine code
questions.explain: Hand-written assembly is used for low-level functions, performance-critical code, and direct access to architecture features such as specific registers. It is not portable, and compilers do translate C to machine code.

questions.q: A programmer can sometimes write assembly code that runs faster than the compiler's optimized assembly translation of C.
questions.explain: Sometimes hand-written assembly beats the compiler's optimized output, which is one reason performance-critical code is sometimes written in assembly.

questions.q: Most operating system code is written in assembly.
questions.explain: Only small parts of an operating system are usually written in assembly. Nearly all OS code is written in C, relying on good optimizing compilers.

questions.q: Why is nearly all operating system code written in C rather than assembly?
choices: C always runs faster than any hand-written assembly
Operating systems are not allowed to contain any assembly code
C is portable and much higher level, and good optimizing compilers produce machine code that performs well
questions.explain: C is portable and much higher level than assembly, and optimizing compilers produce fast machine code. Small parts of an OS are still written in assembly.

questions.q: Even if you rarely write assembly, being able to read a program's assembly code helps with which of the following?
choices: Discovering and understanding security vulnerabilities in programs
Getting a deeper understanding of what a program does and how it executes
Making the C source code portable to other architectures
Avoiding the need to use a compiler
questions.explain: Reading assembly gives a deeper understanding of what a program does and how it runs, and helps you understand performance and find security vulnerabilities.
